history.q: Which Mauryan emperor embraced Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga War?
history.fact: His Lion Capital at Sarnath, carved over 2,200 years ago, is now India's national emblem.

history.q: In which year did India gain independence from British rule?
history.fact: Nehru marked the moment in his 'Tryst with Destiny' speech, delivered at the stroke of midnight on 14-15 August 1947.

history.q: Who led the 1930 Salt March to Dandi in protest against the British salt tax?
history.fact: The march covered about 385 km from Sabarmati Ashram in 24 days; at Dandi, Gandhi picked up a lump of natural salt from the shore.

history.q: Which ruler founded the Mughal Empire after winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
history.fact: Babur wrote a vivid memoir, the Baburnama, in Chagatai Turkic, describing everything from battles to India's fruits.

history.q: Which Harappan site in Gujarat is famous for what is often described as one of the world's earliest known dockyards?
history.fact: Indus Valley cities were remarkably well planned, with grid-like streets and covered drains, more than 4,000 years ago.

history.q: The Indian Rebellion of 1857 began with a sepoy uprising in which town?
history.fact: Often called India's First War of Independence, it led the British Crown to take direct rule from the East India Company in 1858.

history.q: The 1757 Battle of Plassey gave the British East India Company control over which region?
history.fact: Robert Clive's victory over Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah was helped by the defection of the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar.

history.q: Which ancient Buddhist monastic university in Bihar, where the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied in the 7th century, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
history.fact: Nalanda drew students from across Asia; its excavated ruins include red-brick monasteries, temples and shrines.

history.q: Which South Indian dynasty, under Rajendra I, sent a naval expedition against Srivijaya in Southeast Asia around 1025 CE?
history.fact: Rajendra I built a new capital, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, meaning 'the city of the Chola who conquered the Ganges'.

history.q: Which Gupta emperor is celebrated in the Allahabad Pillar inscription composed by the poet Harishena?
history.fact: Some of his gold coins show him playing a veena, hinting at a ruler who prized music as well as conquest.

history.q: Which Mughal emperor, famed for religious tolerance, built the city of Fatehpur Sikri?
history.fact: Akbar held debates among scholars of many faiths at Fatehpur Sikri's Ibadat Khana, or "House of Worship".

history.q: Which Maratha ruler was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674?
history.fact: Shivaji built and captured a network of hill and sea forts, and is often credited with founding a Maratha navy.

history.q: Which Portuguese navigator reached Calicut by sea in 1498?
history.fact: Da Gama's voyage opened the first all-sea route from Europe to India, around Africa's Cape of Good Hope.

history.q: Which queen of Jhansi became a celebrated heroine of the 1857 rebellion?
history.fact: Lakshmibai died fighting near Gwalior in 1858; a British officer described her as the most dangerous of the rebel leaders.

history.q: In which city did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place in 1919?
history.fact: Rabindranath Tagore gave up his British knighthood in protest at the massacre.

history.q: Who founded the Maurya Empire around 321 BCE?
history.fact: According to Jain tradition, Chandragupta gave up his throne and became an ascetic at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.

history.q: Which Mughal emperor, who died in 1707, ruled the empire at its greatest territorial extent?
history.fact: Aurangzeb reigned for 49 years; his simple tomb at Khuldabad in Maharashtra is open to the sky.

history.q: Which South Indian empire had its capital at Hampi, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
history.fact: Foreign visitors in the 1500s compared Vijayanagara to Rome and described its markets heaped with diamonds and rubies.

history.q: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
history.fact: The first session met in Bombay with 72 delegates; one of its founders was a retired British civil servant, Allan Octavian Hume.

history.q: In which year did Gandhi launch the Quit India Movement?
history.fact: Gandhi's Quit India speech in Bombay urged Indians to "Do or Die"; most Congress leaders were arrested the next morning.

history.q: Which Delhi Sultanate ruler moved his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan?
history.fact: Muhammad bin Tughluq also tried a token currency of brass and copper coins, which was soon undone by mass forgery.

history.q: Who ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240, the only woman to do so?
history.fact: Razia was chosen as heir by her father Iltutmish, who reportedly judged her more capable than her brothers.

history.q: Which Governor-General applied the "Doctrine of Lapse" to annex states such as Satara and Jhansi?
history.fact: Dalhousie also oversaw India's first passenger railway, which ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853.

history.q: Which Chalukya king defeated the emperor Harsha on the banks of the Narmada?
history.fact: Pulakeshin's victories are recorded in the Aihole inscription, composed in Sanskrit by the poet Ravikirti.

history.q: Which 1916 agreement brought the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League together on reform demands?
history.fact: The Lucknow Pact was agreed at sessions of both parties held in the same city in December 1916.

technology.q: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named after which ancient mathematician-astronomer?
technology.fact: It was launched on a Soviet rocket. Its namesake, born in 476 CE, proposed that the Earth spins on its own axis.

technology.q: Which self-taught mathematician from Tamil Nadu worked with G. H. Hardy at Cambridge?
technology.fact: Hardy once called his taxi number, 1729, dull; Ramanujan replied it is the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two ways.

technology.q: Which Indian city is often called the 'Silicon Valley of India'?
technology.fact: The city is also home to the headquarters of ISRO, India's space agency.

technology.q: Which aerospace scientist, nicknamed the 'Missile Man of India', became the country's President in 2002?
technology.fact: He earlier led the SLV-3 project, India's first satellite launch vehicle, which put the Rohini satellite into orbit in 1980.

technology.q: Which 7th-century mathematician wrote the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, setting out early rules for calculating with zero?
technology.fact: Written in 628 CE, it treats zero as a number in its own right and gives rules for negative numbers, which he called 'debts'.

technology.q: C. V. Raman won the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering an effect involving the scattering of what?
technology.fact: India celebrates National Science Day on 28 February, the date in 1928 when he announced the Raman effect.

technology.q: Who is widely regarded as the father of India's space programme?
technology.fact: The Moon landers of both Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 were named 'Vikram' in his honour.

technology.q: The particle name 'boson' honours which Indian physicist?
technology.fact: Einstein translated Bose's 1924 paper into German and had it published, giving rise to Bose-Einstein statistics.

technology.q: Which ancient Indian physician is traditionally credited with a treatise describing early techniques for reconstructing the nose?
technology.fact: The Sushruta Samhita, a classic text of Ayurveda, describes surgical instruments and procedures in striking detail.

technology.q: Which scientist invented the crescograph, a device for measuring plant growth?
technology.fact: He was also a pioneer of radio and microwave research in the 1890s, and founded Kolkata's Bose Institute in 1917.

technology.q: India's Mars Orbiter Mission, launched in 2013, is popularly known by what name?
technology.fact: It made India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit, and the first to succeed on its first attempt.

technology.q: What is the name of India's national space agency?
technology.fact: ISRO was founded in 1969; in India's first rocket launches at Thumba, parts were famously carried to the pad on bicycles.

technology.q: The place-value number system used worldwide today, including zero, is commonly called what?
technology.fact: The system reached Europe via Arabic texts; Fibonacci promoted it in his 1202 book Liber Abaci.

technology.q: Which Indian company launched the Nano, marketed as the world's cheapest car, in 2009?
technology.fact: The Nano launched at a base price of 1 lakh rupees, about US$2,000 at the time.

technology.q: Which India-born executive became CEO of Google in 2015?
technology.fact: Pichai grew up in Chennai and studied metallurgical engineering at IIT Kharagpur.

technology.q: Which physicist is known as the father of India's nuclear programme?
technology.fact: India's main nuclear research centre in Mumbai, the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, is named after him.

technology.q: Which India-born astrophysicist shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on the evolution of stars?
technology.fact: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory, launched in 1999, is named in his honour.

technology.q: Which agricultural scientist is known as the father of India's Green Revolution?
technology.fact: High-yield wheat and rice helped India move from food shortages to self-sufficiency in grain by the 1970s.

technology.q: Which dairy cooperative brand is associated with Verghese Kurien and India's "White Revolution"?
technology.fact: Amul began in Anand, Gujarat, in 1946; Operation Flood helped make India the world's largest milk producer.

technology.q: What is the name of India's instant mobile payment system, launched in 2016?
technology.fact: UPI, the Unified Payments Interface, lets people pay by scanning a QR code, and even small street vendors display one.

technology.q: What was the code name of India's first nuclear test, conducted at Pokhran in 1974?
technology.fact: The test was carried out on 18 May 1974, which that year was Buddha Purnima, the festival marking the Buddha's birth.

technology.q: Which 14th-century mathematician, founder of the Kerala school, developed infinite series for trigonometric functions?
technology.fact: Madhava's series for pi and sine predate similar European results by around 250 years.

technology.q: Which statistician founded the Indian Statistical Institute in 1931?
technology.fact: The Mahalanobis distance, still used in machine learning, is named after him; his birthday is India's Statistics Day.

technology.q: Which India-born scientist shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studies of the ribosome?
technology.fact: Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories; mapping them helps in designing new antibiotics.

technology.q: What was the name of the high-carbon crucible steel from South India prized for sword blades?
technology.fact: Wootz ingots were traded to the Middle East, where smiths forged them into the famous rippled "Damascus" blades.

art.q: Which Mughal emperor commissioned the Taj Mahal as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
art.fact: Its white marble is inlaid with semi-precious stones in floral patterns, a technique known as pietra dura.

art.q: Which classical dance form originated in the temples of Tamil Nadu?
art.fact: It is usually performed to Carnatic music and uses expressive hand gestures called mudras to tell stories.

art.q: Which sitar virtuoso taught George Harrison of The Beatles and performed at Woodstock in 1969?
art.fact: He won several Grammy Awards, and his daughters are the sitarist Anoushka Shankar and the singer Norah Jones.

art.q: What nickname is commonly used for the Hindi-language film industry based in Mumbai?
art.fact: India produces more feature films each year than any other country, in many languages beyond Hindi.

art.q: For which collection of poems is Rabindranath Tagore best known, central to his 1913 Nobel Prize?
art.fact: He was the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature and wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

art.q: What was Satyajit Ray's acclaimed debut feature film, released in 1955?
art.fact: Ray received an Honorary Academy Award in 1992 for his lifetime of filmmaking.

art.q: Which cave complex in Maharashtra is renowned for ancient Buddhist murals, some more than 2,000 years old?
art.fact: The caves lay largely forgotten until 1819, when a British officer came across them during a tiger hunt.

art.q: Which 19th-century painter from Kerala became famous for depicting Indian mythological scenes with European oil-painting techniques?
art.fact: His lithographic press made affordable prints of his paintings, bringing his images of gods and goddesses into homes across India.

art.q: Which dynasty built the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora in the 8th century?
art.fact: The temple was carved from the top down out of a single basalt cliff, making it one of the largest monolithic structures in the world.

art.q: Which classical poet wrote the Sanskrit play Abhijnanashakuntalam (The Recognition of Shakuntala)?
art.fact: William Jones's 1789 English translation enchanted European readers, including the German poet Goethe.

art.q: Which Sanskrit epic tells the story of Prince Rama and his wife Sita?
art.fact: The Ramayana is traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki and is retold in versions across Southeast Asia.

art.q: Which classical dance-drama from Kerala is known for elaborate green face make-up and huge headdresses?
art.fact: Kathakali performers train their eye muscles for years so they can express emotions without speaking.

art.q: Which 13th-century temple in Odisha is designed as a giant chariot for the sun god?
art.fact: The temple's 24 carved stone wheels work as sundials; you can read the time from their shadows.

art.q: Which pair of hand drums is central to Hindustani classical music?
art.fact: Ustad Zakir Hussain, the most famous tabla player of recent times, won several Grammy Awards.

art.q: Which Hindi film star is nicknamed "Big B"?
art.fact: Bachchan's 1970s "angry young man" roles made him a superstar; he also hosts India's version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire.

art.q: Which author won the 1981 Booker Prize for "Midnight's Children"?
art.fact: The novel's narrator is born at the exact moment of India's independence, midnight on 15 August 1947.

art.q: Which playback singer, awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2001, sang the patriotic song "Ae Mere Watan Ke Logon"?
art.fact: When she sang it in 1963, Prime Minister Nehru was reportedly moved to tears.

art.q: Which 16th-century garden tomb in Delhi is often seen as a forerunner of the Taj Mahal?
art.fact: It was the first grand garden tomb in India, built for Humayun on the orders of his widow, Bega Begum.

art.q: Which Swiss-French architect planned the city of Chandigarh in the 1950s?
art.fact: Chandigarh's symbol, the Open Hand Monument, was designed by Le Corbusier as a sign of peace and reconciliation.

art.q: Which composer won two Oscars for "Slumdog Millionaire" in 2009?
art.fact: Rahman began as a session keyboard player and jingle composer before his breakthrough film score for Roja in 1992.

art.q: Madhubani painting comes from the Mithila region, mostly in which Indian state?
art.fact: Madhubani art was traditionally painted by women on freshly plastered mud walls for weddings and festivals.

art.q: Which ancient Tamil epic tells the story of Kannagi, who avenges her husband's wrongful execution?
art.fact: Its title means "the tale of the anklet", after the jewelled anklet at the heart of the plot.

art.q: Which composer, one of the "Trinity" of Carnatic music, wrote thousands of devotional songs in Telugu?
art.fact: Every January, musicians gather at his shrine in Thiruvaiyaru to sing his five most famous compositions together.

art.q: Which Indian architect won the Pritzker Prize in 2018?
art.fact: Doshi worked with Le Corbusier in Paris and Ahmedabad and designed low-cost housing for tens of thousands of people.

art.q: Which 1957 film was India's first nominee for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film?
art.fact: Mother India lost the Oscar by a single vote to Fellini's "Nights of Cabiria", according to its director.

politics.q: Who was India's first Prime Minister?
politics.fact: Serving from 1947 until his death in 1964, he remains India's longest-serving Prime Minister.

politics.q: On which date does India celebrate Republic Day?
politics.fact: The Constitution took effect on 26 January 1950; it is the longest written national constitution in the world.

politics.q: What is the name of the lower house of India's Parliament?
politics.fact: Lok Sabha means 'House of the People'. Most members of the upper house, the Rajya Sabha, are elected by state legislatures.

politics.q: Who was India's first woman Prime Minister?
politics.fact: Nehru's daughter, she served as Prime Minister from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 to 1984.

politics.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of India's Constitution?
politics.fact: A jurist, economist and social reformer, Ambedkar was also independent India's first Law Minister.

politics.q: Who was the first President of India?
politics.fact: He is the only President to have served two full terms, from 1950 to 1962.

politics.q: Which leader is credited with integrating hundreds of princely states into India after independence?
politics.fact: He is honoured by the Statue of Unity in Gujarat; at 182 m it is the world's tallest statue.

politics.q: Since a constitutional amendment passed in 1988, what is the minimum voting age in India?
politics.fact: The 61st Amendment lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, adding tens of millions of young people to the electoral rolls.

politics.q: The Emergency declared in India in June 1975 ended in which year?
politics.fact: The 44th Amendment of 1978 added safeguards that made it harder to declare an emergency in future.

politics.q: On which date did the Constituent Assembly adopt India's Constitution, now marked as Constitution Day?
politics.fact: The original copies, hand-calligraphed in English and Hindi, are kept in helium-filled cases in the Parliament library.

politics.q: What is the name of the upper house of India's Parliament?
politics.fact: The Rajya Sabha is never fully dissolved; about a third of its members retire every two years.

politics.q: Which Indian Prime Minister was assassinated in 1991?
politics.fact: Rajiv Gandhi became Prime Minister at 40 in 1984, the youngest person to hold the office.

politics.q: What is the capital of India?
politics.fact: Calcutta was the capital of British India until 1911; New Delhi, designed by Edwin Lutyens, was inaugurated in 1931.

politics.q: Narendra Modi belongs to which political party?
politics.fact: Before becoming Prime Minister in 2014, Modi was Chief Minister of Gujarat for more than 12 years.

politics.q: Which economist served as India's Prime Minister from 2004 to 2014?
politics.fact: As finance minister in 1991, Singh launched the reforms that opened up India's economy.

politics.q: Who became India's first woman President in 2007?
politics.fact: Pratibha Patil was also the first woman Governor of Rajasthan before becoming President.

politics.q: India's national motto "Satyameva Jayate" means what?
politics.fact: The phrase comes from the ancient Mundaka Upanishad and is inscribed below the Lion Capital emblem.

politics.q: Which Prime Minister coined the slogan "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" (Hail the soldier, hail the farmer)?
politics.fact: Shastri raised the slogan in 1965, during war and food shortages; he died in Tashkent in 1966 after signing a peace accord.

politics.q: Which constitutional body conducts national and state elections in India?
politics.fact: For the 1951-52 first general election, symbols were put on ballot boxes so voters who could not read could take part.

politics.q: Which ancient scholar is traditionally credited with the Arthashastra, a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft and economics?
politics.fact: The Arthashastra was rediscovered in 1905 when a palm-leaf manuscript was identified in Mysore.

politics.q: Who was the only Indian to serve as Governor-General of independent India?
politics.fact: He held the post from 1948 until the office was abolished when India became a republic in 1950.

politics.q: In which year did the States Reorganisation Act redraw India's state boundaries largely along linguistic lines?
politics.fact: The push began after Potti Sriramulu's 1952 fast for a Telugu-speaking state, which led to Andhra State in 1953.

politics.q: Which constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to panchayati raj, India's rural local government?
politics.fact: It also reserved at least one-third of panchayat seats for women, bringing over a million women into local office.

politics.q: Which 1976 constitutional amendment added the words "socialist" and "secular" to India's Preamble?
politics.fact: The 42nd Amendment was so sweeping that it is sometimes nicknamed the "mini-Constitution".

politics.q: Who was the first Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
politics.fact: Mavalankar is often called the father of the Lok Sabha for setting many of its rules and traditions.

current-affairs.q: Which Indian mission landed near the Moon's south pole in August 2023?
current-affairs.fact: India became the first country to land near the lunar south pole and the fourth to achieve a soft landing on the Moon.

current-affairs.q: Who was sworn in as India's Prime Minister in June 2024 after that year's general election?
current-affairs.fact: It was Modi's third consecutive term, a feat previously achieved only by Jawaharlal Nehru.

current-affairs.q: According to UN estimates, India overtook which country in 2023 to become the world's most populous nation?
current-affairs.fact: UN figures put India's population at more than 1.42 billion by mid-2023, edging past China's.

current-affairs.q: Which athlete won India's first Olympic gold medal in track and field, in the javelin at the Tokyo Games held in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: His winning throw measured 87.58 m, and he added a silver medal at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

current-affairs.q: What is the name of India's first space mission dedicated to studying the Sun, which reached its observation point in January 2024?
current-affairs.fact: It orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point L1, about 1.5 million km from Earth, where it can watch the Sun without interruption.

current-affairs.q: At the G20 summit hosted in New Delhi in September 2023, which organization was admitted as a permanent member?
current-affairs.fact: The summit was held at Bharat Mandapam, a new convention centre in New Delhi.

current-affairs.q: Which team did India defeat in the final of the 2024 ICC Men's T20 World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: The final was played in Barbados; it was India's second T20 World Cup title after winning the first tournament in 2007.

current-affairs.q: Which Indian player became the youngest undisputed World Chess Champion in December 2024?
current-affairs.fact: Aged 18, he defeated China's Ding Liren in Singapore, becoming India's second world champion after Viswanathan Anand.

current-affairs.q: The Atal Setu, opened in January 2024 as India's longest sea bridge, serves which metropolitan region?
current-affairs.fact: Also called the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, the roughly 21.8 km bridge crosses the harbour from Sewri to Navi Mumbai.

current-affairs.q: In 2021, which Harappan city in Gujarat was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
current-affairs.fact: The same year, Telangana's Ramappa Temple, a 13th-century Kakatiya masterpiece, also joined the World Heritage list.

current-affairs.q: The song "Naatu Naatu", which won the Oscar for Best Original Song in March 2023, comes from which Telugu film?
current-affairs.fact: It was the first song from an Indian-made film to win an Academy Award.

current-affairs.q: In August 2019, India ended the special constitutional status of which region under Article 370?
current-affairs.fact: The former state was reorganised into two union territories: Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

current-affairs.q: Which team beat India in the final of the 2023 Men's Cricket World Cup in Ahmedabad?
current-affairs.fact: Travis Head's century won Australia its sixth men's World Cup, in front of a crowd of over 90,000.

current-affairs.q: In 2020, India banned which hugely popular short-video app along with dozens of other apps?
current-affairs.fact: India had been TikTok's largest market by users; Instagram Reels and Indian apps rushed to fill the gap.

current-affairs.q: Who became India's President in July 2022, the first person from a tribal community to hold the office?
current-affairs.fact: Murmu, from Odisha's Santal community, was earlier the first woman to serve as Governor of Jharkhand.

current-affairs.q: Which team did India beat in the final of the 2025 ICC Champions Trophy?
current-affairs.fact: The final was played in Dubai, and the win gave India a record third Champions Trophy title.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, Delhi's ceremonial avenue Rajpath was renamed what?
current-affairs.fact: The avenue runs from Rashtrapati Bhavan to India Gate and hosts the Republic Day parade each January.

current-affairs.q: In which sport did Manu Bhaker win two bronze medals at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: She became the first Indian since independence to win two medals at a single Olympic Games.

current-affairs.q: A 2023 law reserves what share of seats in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for women?
current-affairs.fact: The idea had been debated for nearly three decades before the law, called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, was passed.

current-affairs.q: In June 2025, Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian astronaut to visit which orbiting station?
current-affairs.fact: He was the first Indian in space since Rakesh Sharma flew to the Soviet station Salyut 7 in 1984.

current-affairs.q: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force from July 2024, replaced which colonial-era law?
current-affairs.fact: The Indian Penal Code had been in force since 1862 and was drafted under the historian Thomas Babington Macaulay.

current-affairs.q: Which Indian player won the FIDE Women's World Cup in chess in July 2025?
current-affairs.fact: The final was an all-Indian match against Koneru Humpy, and victory also earned the 19-year-old the grandmaster title.

current-affairs.q: The new Pamban Bridge, India's first vertical-lift sea bridge, opened in April 2025 to link the mainland with which island town?
current-affairs.fact: It replaced a 1914 railway bridge whose two central leaves were raised by hand to let ships pass.

current-affairs.q: In January 2025, which state became the first since independence to enact and implement its own Uniform Civil Code?
current-affairs.fact: Goa already had a common civil code inherited from Portuguese rule, which it kept after joining India in 1961.

current-affairs.q: In 2023, India's "Operation Kaveri" evacuated its citizens from which country?
current-affairs.fact: Indian Navy ships and Air Force planes ferried evacuees from Port Sudan to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia.

society.q: In November 2021, India repealed three controversial laws passed in 2020 concerning what?
society.fact: The repeal followed a year-long protest by farmers camped on the edges of Delhi, one of the largest demonstrations in India's recent history.

society.q: India's nationwide lockdown announced on 24 March 2020 was initially set to last how many days?
society.fact: It was extended several times into June, and prompted millions of migrant workers to leave cities for their home villages.

society.q: In May 2023, the Reserve Bank of India announced the withdrawal of which banknote from circulation?
society.fact: The note had been introduced after the 2016 demonetisation; over 97% of the notes were returned to banks within a year.

society.q: In 2021, petrol prices in many Indian cities crossed which per-litre milestone for the first time?
society.fact: Taxes made up over half the pump price; the central government later cut excise duty in November 2021 and May 2022 to ease the burden.

society.q: In 2022, India overtook which country to become the world's fifth-largest economy?
society.fact: By 2025 India was widely reported to have passed Japan for fourth place, though its GDP per person remains far lower than either.

society.q: A scheme begun in 2020 and extended to 2028 gives free food grain each month to roughly how many Indians?
society.fact: PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana started as pandemic relief with 5 kg of rice or wheat per person; it was made free of charge and extended for five years in 2024.

society.q: In 2023, India remained the world's largest recipient of remittances, receiving roughly how much?
society.fact: The World Bank estimated about $125 billion, with the United States, Gulf states and the UK the main sources.

society.q: In July 2022, the Indian rupee weakened past which level against the US dollar for the first time?
society.fact: It followed rising US interest rates and oil prices; the rupee went on to pass 85 to the dollar in December 2024.

society.q: The 2025 Union Budget made annual income up to how much effectively free of income tax under the new regime?
society.fact: The threshold was raised from ₹7 lakh; a 'lakh' is 100,000, so ₹12 lakh is about 1.2 million rupees.

society.q: The Reserve Bank of India targets inflation of 4% with a tolerance band of how much either side?
society.fact: The 2-6% band was set in 2016; inflation stayed above 6% for most of 2022, forcing the RBI to explain itself to the government.

society.q: India's National Family Health Survey for 2019-21 found the total fertility rate had fallen to what?
society.fact: That is below the replacement level of 2.1 for the first time, though rates stay higher in states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

society.q: India's official unemployment rate in the 2022-23 Periodic Labour Force Survey was roughly what?
society.fact: The low headline figure of 3.2% masks high youth unemployment and widespread informal or self-employed work.

society.q: The ILO's 2024 India Employment Report found young people made up roughly what share of India's unemployed?
society.fact: The report also found unemployment was highest among educated youth, with graduates far more likely to be jobless than those with no schooling.

society.q: Launched in 2019, the PM-KISAN scheme pays farming families how much per year?
society.fact: The money arrives in three instalments straight into bank accounts and reaches over 90 million farming households.

society.q: From October 2019, which group was given free travel on Delhi's public buses?
society.fact: Passengers receive a 'pink ticket' for each free ride; Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Punjab later launched similar schemes.

society.q: India's retail inflation peaked in April 2022 at roughly what level, its highest in eight years?
society.fact: Food and fuel led the rise after the war in Ukraine; in 2023 tomato prices briefly rose more than fivefold, becoming a national talking point.

society.q: The Agnipath scheme, introduced in 2022, recruits soldiers for a fixed term of how many years?
society.fact: Only a quarter of each batch of 'Agniveers' is retained afterwards; the scheme triggered protests from young people seeking military careers.

society.q: In August 2023, India's UPI payment system crossed how many transactions in a single month for the first time?
society.fact: QR-code payments are now accepted by street vendors across India, and UPI handles more transactions than Visa does worldwide.

society.q: India's census, last held in 2011 and delayed from 2021, was scheduled in 2025 to be completed in which year?
society.fact: The reference date is 1 March 2027, and for the first time since 1931 the count will record every person's caste.

society.q: In September 2025, India simplified GST to two main rates: 5% and what?
society.fact: The 12% and 28% slabs were scrapped and a 40% rate kept for luxury and 'sin' goods; everyday items such as soap and small cars got cheaper.

society.q: The four labour codes India brought into force in November 2025 replaced roughly how many older labour laws?
society.fact: The codes, passed by Parliament in 2019 and 2020, cover wages, social security, industrial relations and workplace safety, including gig workers.

society.q: NITI Aayog estimated in 2024 that roughly how many Indians escaped multidimensional poverty between 2013-14 and 2022-23?
society.fact: The multidimensional index measures deprivation in health, education and living standards rather than income alone.

society.q: A 2022 NITI Aayog report estimated India had roughly how many gig workers in 2020-21?
society.fact: It projected the number would reach over 23 million by 2030; a 2020 social security code was the first to formally define gig and platform work.

society.q: The Unified Pension Scheme, in force from April 2025, assures central government staff a pension of what share of their final-year average pay?
society.fact: It answered demands to restore the old pension scheme replaced in 2004, and requires at least 25 years of service for the full amount.

society.q: In 2024, the Ayushman Bharat health insurance scheme was extended to all Indians above what age, regardless of income?
society.fact: The scheme gives families ₹5 lakh a year of hospital cover; the extension added about 60 million older people.

general.q: What is India's national animal?
general.fact: India is home to roughly three-quarters of the world's wild tigers.

general.q: Which sacred river flows past the ghats of Varanasi?
general.fact: Varanasi is often described as one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities.

general.q: In which sport has India won eight Olympic gold medals, including six in a row from 1928 to 1956?
general.fact: The star of that golden era, Dhyan Chand, is so revered that India's National Sports Day, 29 August, marks his birthday.

general.q: Which festival, celebrated with oil lamps and fireworks, is known as the 'festival of lights'?
general.fact: Diwali is celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists, usually in October or November.

general.q: Kangchenjunga, on India's border with Nepal, ranks where among the world's highest mountains?
general.fact: Out of respect for local beliefs, many climbers traditionally stop just short of its true summit.

general.q: Dosa, the South Indian crepe, is traditionally made from a fermented batter of rice and which legume?
general.fact: Fermenting the batter overnight gives dosa its tangy flavour and light, crisp texture.

general.q: Which vast mangrove forest, shared with Bangladesh, is home to tigers that swim between islands?
general.fact: Formed in the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers, it is the largest mangrove forest in the world.

general.q: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, among the wettest places on Earth, are in which Indian state?
general.fact: Khasi communities there grow 'living root bridges' by guiding the roots of rubber fig trees across streams.

general.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of India's Constitution?
general.fact: The list began with 14 languages in 1950 and has grown through amendments; the most recent additions came in 2003.

general.q: Which Indian state has the longest coastline?
general.fact: Inland from Gujarat's long coast lies Gir forest, the last wild home of the Asiatic lion.

general.q: What is India's national bird?
general.fact: Only the male peafowl has the famous train of feathers, which can make up more than 60% of its body length.

general.q: The Golden Temple in Amritsar is the holiest shrine of which religion?
general.fact: The Golden Temple's community kitchen serves free meals to tens of thousands of visitors every day.

general.q: Which board game is generally traced back to the ancient Indian game chaturanga?
general.fact: Chaturanga means "four divisions" of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, the ancestors of chess pieces.

general.q: Which small Indian state, a Portuguese colony until 1961, is famous for its beaches?
general.fact: Portuguese rule in Goa lasted about 450 years, longer than British rule anywhere in India.

general.q: Which spring festival is celebrated by throwing coloured powder and water?
general.fact: Holi bonfires are lit on the night before the colours, recalling the legend of Prahlad and Holika.

general.q: Which desert lies mostly in the state of Rajasthan?
general.fact: The Thar is one of the most densely populated deserts in the world.

general.q: Which part of India is famous for growing saffron?
general.fact: It takes about 150,000 crocus flowers, each picked by hand, to produce one kilogram of saffron.

general.q: Which Indian state is the country's largest tea-producing region, known for its strong, malty black tea?
general.fact: In 1823 Robert Bruce was shown tea plants growing wild in Assam, used by local Singpho people.

general.q: Which Indian city is known as the "Pink City"?
general.fact: Jaipur was painted pink, a colour of hospitality, to welcome the Prince of Wales in 1876, and the tradition stuck.

general.q: Which town lies at the southern tip of mainland India, where three seas meet?
general.fact: At Kanyakumari the Arabian Sea, Indian Ocean and Bay of Bengal meet, and on full-moon evenings the sun can set as the moon rises.

general.q: Chilika, Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, lies in which Indian state?
general.fact: Chilika is a winter home to huge flocks of migratory birds and to rare Irrawaddy dolphins.

general.q: What is the name of India's southernmost point, on Great Nicobar Island?
general.fact: Indira Point lies closer to Indonesia's Sumatra than to mainland India.

general.q: Loktak Lake, famous for its floating islands called phumdis, is in which state?
general.fact: Keibul Lamjao, the world's only floating national park, sits on Loktak's phumdis and protects the rare sangai deer.

general.q: Majuli, one of the world's largest river islands, lies in which river?
general.fact: Majuli is home to centuries-old Vaishnavite monasteries called satras, known for dance, drama and mask-making.

general.q: Which river is often called the "Dakshin Ganga", or Ganges of the South?
general.fact: The Godavari rises near Nashik in Maharashtra and flows about 1,465 km east to the Bay of Bengal.
